nameStory: The 'roundleaf' part of this ragwort's name comes from its distinctive spoon-shaped basal leaves that are much rounder than other ragworts. The name 'ragwort' itself refers to the ragged, divided appearance of the upper leaves on the flowering stem. It's like the plant can't decide whether it wants round leaves or raggedy ones, so it does both!
description: Roundleaf ragwort is a cheerful spring wildflower that stands about 1-2 feet tall with bright yellow daisy-like blooms. What makes it special is its two-faced personality when it comes to leaves - the bottom leaves are rounded and spoon-shaped, while the upper leaves are deeply divided and feathery. The sunny yellow flowers cluster together at the top of sturdy stems, creating a golden crown that rises well above the foliage. It's a perennial that comes back year after year, bringing early color to woodland edges.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: The most telling feature - basal leaves are distinctly spoon-shaped or obovate (wider at the tip) with toothed edges that feel slightly fuzzy, while stem leaves are deeply divided into narrow segments like fingers on a hand

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow daisy-like flowers about 3/4 inch across with cheerful yellow petals (ray flowers) surrounding orange-yellow centers (disk flowers), clustered in flat-topped groups

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Erect stems rise 1-2 feet tall, holding the flower clusters well above the basal rosette of rounded leaves, giving it a tidy, organized appearance

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Smooth, often reddish-tinged stems that feel firm and slightly succulent when gently squeezed, branching near the top to support the flower clusters

habitat: Roundleaf ragwort thrives in partially shaded areas like woodland edges, open woods, and rocky slopes throughout New England. It prefers well-drained, often rocky or sandy soils and can tolerate some drought once established. Look for it in transitional areas between forest and field, often growing alongside wild columbine and early saxifrage.

seasonality.spring: Peak blooming season from April to early June, when the bright yellow flowers are most prominent and the contrast between round basal leaves and divided stem leaves is most obvious.
seasonality.summer: Flowers fade and plants may go dormant in hot, dry conditions, though basal leaves often persist in cooler, moister spots.
seasonality.fall: Plants may send up new basal leaves, and seed heads with fluffy white bristles help identify spent plants.
seasonality.winter: Mostly dormant with little visible above ground, though occasional basal leaf rosettes may persist under snow in milder areas.

funFact: This plant is like a botanical shape-shifter - scientists have discovered that the dramatic difference between its round bottom leaves and deeply divided top leaves helps it capture maximum sunlight at ground level early in the season, then switch to a different leaf shape that works better when the plant is tall and competing with other vegetation!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with golden ragwort, but roundleaf ragwort's basal leaves are truly spoon-shaped and wider at the tip, while golden ragwort's are more heart-shaped with a notched base. Memory trick: 'Roundleaf = spoon for stirring soup, golden = heart-shaped like love.'
contextualKnowledge: Like other ragworts, this plant was historically used in folk medicine but contains compounds that can be toxic to livestock and humans if consumed in large quantities. The genus was recently moved from Senecio to Packera, so you might see it listed under both names in older field guides.
compareHints: Among its ragwort relatives, roundleaf ragwort is distinguished by its truly spoon-shaped basal leaves - golden ragwort has heart-shaped leaves, while New England ragwort has more oval leaves that taper to both ends. Balsam ragwort tends to grow in wetter areas and has more consistently divided leaves throughout the plant.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Golden ragwort stands out from its ragwort relatives by its distinctive heart-shaped basal leaves - roundleaf ragwort has more rounded leaves, while New England ragwort has more deeply cut basal leaves.

New England ragwort stands out among its Packera relatives by its distinctively narrow, lance-shaped basal leaves - golden ragwort has heart-shaped leaves, roundleaf ragwort has round to oval leaves, and butterweed has more deeply lobed leaves.
Among New England's ragworts, balsam ragwort is distinguished by its preference for consistently wet habitats and its more irregularly divided, raggedy-looking leaves.
Among its ragwort relatives, butterweed stands out for its deeply divided, cress-like leaves - golden ragwort has heart-shaped basal leaves, while roundleaf ragwort has rounded, less-divided foliage.
